text: Amazon Dynamo (Case Study) Sources: DeCandia et al., "Dynamo: Amazon's Highly Available Key-value Store" (SOSP 2007) Why it was built: Amazon's shopping cart service needed to always accept a write — even during a network partition or node failure — because a customer being unable to add to their cart is a direct lost sale. Traditional strongly-consistent databases prioritize consistency over availability during a partition; Dynamo inverted that priority for this specific use case. Core design goal: always writable. Dynamo chose availability and partition tolerance over strict consistency (the AP side of CAP) — a write should never be rejected because some replicas are temporarily unreachable. This means the system can end up with temporarily conflicting versions of the same data, which it must reconcile later rather than prevent up front. Consistent hashing for partitioning: Data is partitioned across nodes using consistent hashing (each node owns a range on a hash ring). Adding or removing a node only reshuffles the data immediately adjacent to it on the ring, not the entire dataset — critical for a system meant to scale nodes up/down without a massive rebalancing event. Sloppy quorum & hinted handoff: Normally a write requires acknowledgment from W replicas and a read from R replicas (with W + R > N giving strong-ish consistency). But if some of the "correct" replica nodes are down, Dynamo still accepts the write on a different, temporarily-substituting node ("sloppy quorum") rather than rejecting it — the substitute node holds a "hint" to hand the data back to the rightful replica once it recovers (hinted handoff). This is the core mechanism of the "always writable" guarantee. Vector clocks for conflict resolution: Because writes can be accepted by different replicas independently during a partition, the same key can end up with multiple conflicting versions. Dynamo tags each version with a vector clock (tracks which node made which update, in what order) so it can determine if one version is a strict descendant of another (safe to auto-merge) or if they're genuinely concurrent conflicting writes (must be reconciled — Dynamo pushes this reconciliation to the application, e.g. "merge the two shopping carts," since only the application knows how to correctly merge domain data). Read-repair & anti-entropy: When a read encounters divergent versions across replicas, the coordinator can push the resolved/latest version back to the stale replicas ("read repair") instead of waiting for a separate background process — keeps replicas converging toward consistency without blocking writes to do so. Legacy and influence: Dynamo's design (consistent hashing, eventual consistency, vector clocks, "AP over CP" for write availability) directly influenced Cassandra, Riak, and Amazon's own managed DynamoDB — this paper is one of the most cited references in distributed systems design precisely because it made an explicit, well-justified trade-off (availability over consistency) that became a standard pattern to reference when discussing CAP theorem trade-offs in interviews.

text: Bloom Filters Sources: Burton H. Bloom, "Space/Time Trade-offs in Hash Coding with Allowable Errors" (1970), Redis documentation (Bloom Filter / probabilistic data structures) What it is: A probabilistic data structure that answers "have I possibly seen this item before?" using a fixed, tiny amount of memory — regardless of how many items have been added. Trades perfect accuracy for massive space savings. The guarantee (this is the important part): No false negatives: if the filter says "definitely not present," the item is genuinely not present. Possible false positives: if the filter says "possibly present," it might actually not be — the false positive rate is tunable (smaller filter / more items = higher false positive rate). It never says "definitely present" for something that was never added incorrectly in the wrong direction — the asymmetry only goes one way, which is what makes it usable: you only need a secondary, slower check for the "possibly present" case. How it works: A bit array of m bits, all initially 0, plus k independent hash functions. To add an item: hash it k times, set the k resulting bit positions to 1. To check an item: hash it the same k times, if ALL k bit positions are 1, report "possibly present"; if ANY bit is 0, report "definitely not present" (since adding that item would have set that bit). False positives happen because bits get shared/overwritten by other items' hashes — you can't tell whether a set bit was set by the item you're checking or by pure coincidence from other insertions. Why not just use a hash set: A hash set storing millions of actual keys uses far more memory (must store each key or at least its full hash) than a Bloom filter, which only needs a handful of bits per item regardless of key size. The trade is: a hash set has zero false positives, a Bloom filter accepts a small false-positive rate in exchange for a fraction of the memory. Cannot remove items (in the basic version): Because bits are shared across multiple items' hashes, clearing a bit to "remove" one item could break the correctness for other items that also set that bit. A Counting Bloom Filter (using small counters instead of single bits) supports removal at the cost of more memory — used when deletions are actually needed. Real-world example: A CDN or database wants to avoid an expensive disk/network lookup for keys that definitely don't exist (e.g. checking if a URL is on a known-malicious list, or if a cache key might exist before hitting disk). Check the Bloom filter first: if "definitely not present," skip the expensive lookup entirely. If "possibly present," do the real (slower, authoritative) lookup to confirm — the small false-positive rate just means occasionally doing an unnecessary real lookup, never missing an item that's actually there. A regular in-process lock (mutex) doesn't work here because the "processes" are on different machines with no shared memory. Why you need one: Running the same scheduled job twice (duplicate emails sent, duplicate charges). Two nodes both thinking they're the "leader" and both writing conflicting data. Preventing two workers from picking up and processing the same queue item. Redis-based locks (simple case): SET a key with a unique value and an expiry (SET lock_key unique_id NX EX 30). NX means "only set if not exists" — this is the actual locking mechanism. Expiry (EX) prevents a deadlock if the holder crashes before releasing. Release by checking the value matches before deleting (via a Lua script, to make compare-and-delete atomic) — otherwise you might delete a lock some other process acquired after your expiry. Limitation: single Redis node is a single point of failure. If it fails over to a replica before the write is replicated, two clients could both believe they hold the lock. Redlock (multi-node Redis locking): Acquire the lock on a majority of independent Redis nodes (e.g. 3 of 5) within a time budget. Considered "acquired" only if majority succeeds before the clock runs out. More resilient to a single node failing, though it has been debated (Martin Kleppmann's critique) as not being fully safe under clock drift/GC pauses — good enough for "efficiency" locks (avoid duplicate work), not for correctness-critical locks (avoid data corruption). ZooKeeper / etcd-based locks (correctness-critical case): Both are consensus-based stores (using ZAB / Raft respectively) — a write is only acknowledged once a majority of nodes agree, which is much stronger than a single Redis node's guarantee. Leader election pattern: each candidate creates an ephemeral sequential node; the candidate with the lowest sequence number is the leader. If the leader's session dies (crash, network partition), its ephemeral node disappears automatically and the next-lowest candidate becomes leader. Use this when correctness matters more than latency — e.g. only one node should ever be allowed to write to a given shard. Fix: every time a lock is granted, issue a monotonically increasing fencing token. The resource being protected (e.g. storage service) rejects any write that comes with an older token than the last one it saw — this is the actual fix for "lock expired but process is still running" bugs, the lock alone is not sufficient. text: Distributed Transactions: 2PC & Saga Pattern Sources: "Designing Data-Intensive Applications" (Kleppmann) ch.9, microservices.io (Chris Richardson) — "Saga pattern" The problem: A single database transaction (BEGIN...COMMIT) guarantees all-or-nothing across tables in one database. But a "place order" flow in a microservices system might need to update order-service's DB, decrement inventory-service's DB, and charge payment-service's DB — three separate databases, no single transaction can span all of them. Two-Phase Commit (2PC): A coordinator asks every participant to "prepare" (lock resources, confirm it *can* commit, but don't commit yet). If all participants vote yes, coordinator tells everyone to commit. If any vote no, coordinator tells everyone to abort. Guarantees atomicity across multiple resources — either all commit or all abort. Why 2PC is avoided in practice at scale: Blocking: if the coordinator crashes after participants have "prepared" but before sending commit/abort, participants are stuck holding locks indefinitely, waiting for a coordinator that may never come back. Latency: every participant must stay locked and waiting through two full round-trips before any of them can proceed — slow, and doesn't scale well across services owned by different teams with independent uptime. Tight coupling: all participants must be available simultaneously; one slow or down service blocks the whole transaction for everyone. Saga pattern (the common alternative in microservices): Break the transaction into a sequence of local transactions, each with its own compensating action to undo it if a later step fails. Example: (1) order-service creates order [compensate: cancel order], (2) inventory-service reserves stock [compensate: release stock], (3) payment-service charges card [compensate: refund]. Two-Phase Commit (2PC): A coordinator asks every participant to "prepare" (lock resources, confirm it *can* commit, but don't commit yet). If all participants vote yes, coordinator tells everyone to commit. If any vote no, coordinator tells everyone to abort. Guarantees atomicity across multiple resources — either all commit or all abort. Why 2PC is avoided in practice at scale: Blocking: if the coordinator crashes after participants have "prepared" but before sending commit/abort, participants are stuck holding locks indefinitely, waiting for a coordinator that may never come back. Latency: every participant must stay locked and waiting through two full round-trips before any of them can proceed — slow, and doesn't scale well across services owned by different teams with independent uptime. Tight coupling: all participants must be available simultaneously; one slow or down service blocks the whole transaction for everyone. Saga pattern (the common alternative in microservices): Break the transaction into a sequence of local transactions, each with its own compensating action to undo it if a later step fails. Example: (1) order-service creates order [compensate: cancel order], (2) inventory-service reserves stock [compensate: release stock], (3) payment-service charges card [compensate: refund]. If step 3 fails, the saga runs compensations for steps 2 and 1 in reverse — no single distributed lock is ever held across all three. Choreography vs Orchestration (two ways to coordinate a saga): Choreography: each service publishes an event when its step completes, next service reacts to that event — fully decentralized, no single point of control, but harder to see the overall flow/state of "which step is this order on." Orchestration: a central saga orchestrator explicitly tells each service what to do next and tracks the saga's state — easier to reason about and debug, but the orchestrator becomes a piece of infrastructure every saga depends on. Key trade-off vs 2PC: Sagas give up strict atomicity (there IS a window where inventory is reserved but payment hasn't happened yet — visible partial state) in exchange for no blocking locks held across services and independent service availability. This is why sagas are preferred in practice: partial visibility for a short window is an acceptable trade for not letting one service's outage freeze every other service's transactions. Real-world example: Booking a flight + hotel as one "trip" transaction: reserve flight seat, reserve hotel room, charge card. If the hotel is sold out by the time that step runs, the saga triggers a compensating action to release the flight seat that was already reserved — the user never ends up charged for a trip that couldn't be fully booked, without ever holding a lock

text: Database Replication & Failover Sources: PostgreSQL documentation (Replication), MySQL documentation (Replication), "Designing Data-Intensive Applications" (Kleppmann) ch.5 What it is: Replication keeps copies of the same data on multiple database nodes. Goals: survive a node failure without data loss, serve more read traffic than one machine can handle, and keep data closer to users in different regions. Leader-follower (primary-replica) replication: One node (leader) accepts all writes. Writes are streamed to one or more followers, which apply them and can serve read traffic. Most common setup for relational databases (Postgres, MySQL). Synchronous vs asynchronous replication: Synchronous: leader waits for follower to confirm the write before acknowledging the client. Zero data loss on failover, but write latency includes network round-trip to the follower, and the leader stalls if the follower is slow/down. Asynchronous: leader acknowledges the client immediately, follower catches up in the background. Fast writes, but a leader crash before replication completes means recent writes are lost. Semi-synchronous: at least one follower confirms synchronously, rest are async — common middle ground (used by MySQL semi-sync replication). Replication lag: The delay between a write on the leader and it appearing on a follower. Causes "read-your-own-writes" bugs: user updates their profile, immediately reloads the page, request is routed to a lagging follower, sees stale data. Fixed by: routing a user's own reads to the leader for a short window after they write, or reading from the same replica they just wrote through. Failover: When the leader dies, a follower must be promoted to leader. Manual failover: safer, slower — human confirms the old leader is really dead before promoting, avoiding split-brain. Automatic failover: faster recovery, but risk of split-brain — if the network partition means the old leader is alive but unreachable, promoting a new leader means two leaders may accept writes simultaneously, causing conflicting data. Tools like Patroni (Postgres) or Orchestrator (MySQL) use a consensus store (etcd/ZooKeeper) to agree on the new leader safely. Multi-leader and leaderless replication: Multi-leader: multiple nodes accept writes, used across data centers — but requires conflict resolution when the same record is written in two places. Leaderless (e.g. Cassandra, DynamoDB style): client writes to several replicas directly and reads from several, using quorum (W + R > N) to guarantee it sees the latest write. No single leader means no failover pause, but consistency is weaker and requires read-repair for divergent replicas. Real-world example: A typical production Postgres setup: one primary handles all writes, two read replicas serve read-heavy endpoints (e.g. product catalog browsing). Patroni monitors primary health via etcd; if the primary fails a health check, etcd elects a new leader from the replicas and updates DNS/proxy routing automatically — this is what "high availability" means for a database in practice.

text: Distributed Transactions: 2PC & Saga Pattern Sources: "Designing Data-Intensive Applications" (Kleppmann) ch.9, microservices.io (Chris Richardson) — "Saga pattern" The problem: A single database transaction (BEGIN...COMMIT) guarantees all-or-nothing across tables in one database. But a "place order" flow in a microservices system might need to update order-service's DB, decrement inventory-service's DB, and charge payment-service's DB — three separate databases, no single transaction can span all of them. Two-Phase Commit (2PC): A coordinator asks every participant to "prepare" (lock resources, confirm it *can* commit, but don't commit yet). If all participants vote yes, coordinator tells everyone to commit. If any vote no, coordinator tells everyone to abort. Guarantees atomicity across multiple resources — either all commit or all abort. Why 2PC is avoided in practice at scale: Blocking: if the coordinator crashes after participants have "prepared" but before sending commit/abort, participants are stuck holding locks indefinitely, waiting for a coordinator that may never come back. Latency: every participant must stay locked and waiting through two full round-trips before any of them can proceed — slow, and doesn't scale well across services owned by different teams with independent uptime. Tight coupling: all participants must be available simultaneously; one slow or down service blocks the whole transaction for everyone. Saga pattern (the common alternative in microservices): Break the transaction into a sequence of local transactions, each with its own compensating action to undo it if a later step fails. Example: (1) order-service creates order [compensate: cancel order], (2) inventory-service reserves stock [compensate: release stock], (3) payment-service charges card [compensate: refund]. If step 3 fails, the saga runs compensations for steps 2 and 1 in reverse — no single distributed lock is ever held across all three. Choreography vs Orchestration (two ways to coordinate a saga): Choreography: each service publishes an event when its step completes, next service reacts to that event — fully decentralized, no single point of control, but harder to see the overall flow/state of "which step is this order on." Orchestration: a central saga orchestrator explicitly tells each service what to do next and tracks the saga's state — easier to reason about and debug, but the orchestrator becomes a piece of infrastructure every saga depends on. Key trade-off vs 2PC: Sagas give up strict atomicity (there IS a window where inventory is reserved but payment hasn't happened yet — visible partial state) in exchange for no blocking locks held across services and independent service availability. This is why sagas are preferred in practice: partial visibility for a short window is an acceptable trade for not letting one service's outage freeze every other service's transactions. text: Search & Indexing (Inverted Index) Sources: Elasticsearch documentation ("Inverted index"), Apache Lucene documentation What it is: Searching billions of documents for a keyword by scanning each one would be far too slow. Search engines instead build an inverted index ahead of time — a data structure that maps each word to the list of documents containing it — so a search becomes a fast lookup instead of a full scan. Forward index vs inverted index: Forward index: document → list of words it contains (this is the natural way you'd store a document, but useless for "find all docs containing X"). Inverted index: word → list of documents containing it. Flips the mapping so a query for a term is a single lookup, not a scan of every document. Building the index: 1. Tokenization: split text into individual terms ("The quick fox" → ["the", "quick", "fox"]). 2. Normalization: lowercase, remove punctuation, stemming (running → run) so "run", "runs", "running" all match the same index entry. 3. Stop word removal (optional): common words like "the", "is" are often excluded since they match nearly everything and add little search value. 4. For each remaining term, append the document ID (and often position within the document, for phrase search) to that term's posting list. Querying: A search for "quick fox" looks up the posting list for "quick" and for "fox", then intersects them — documents in both lists contain both words. Ranking (which result appears first) typically uses TF-IDF or BM25: term frequency (how often the word appears in this doc) weighted against inverse document frequency (how rare the word is across all docs) — a rare word matching is a stronger signal than a common word matching. Distributed search (how this scales to billions of documents): The full index doesn't fit on one machine. It's split into shards, each holding a subset of documents and its own local inverted index. A query fans out to every shard in parallel, each returns its top-N matches, and a coordinating node merges and re-ranks the combined results — this is exactly how Elasticsearch/Solr scale search across a cluster. Each shard is also typically replicated for both availability and to spread read (query) load across replicas. Real-time-ish updates: New documents don't need a full index rebuild — an update is added as a small new index segment; a background merge process periodically combines small segments into larger ones for query efficiency. This is why "just indexed" documents often show up in search within seconds, not instantly, and why search indexes trade a small delay for much better write throughput. Real-world example: An e-commerce product search: catalog of 50M products is sharded across many nodes. Searching "wireless headphones" fans out to every shard, each returns its best local matches ranked by BM25, coordinator merges and returns the final top 20 — the same pattern used by product search on any major e-commerce site or by Elasticsearch-backed log search internally at a company.

Understanding CAP is fundamental to system design — every database and architectural decision involves these trade-offs. The Three Properties: C — Consistency: Every read returns the most recent write (or an error). If you write a value on node 1 and immediately read it from node 2, you get the updated value. This is "strong consistency." Example: bank account balance — you must see the current balance, not a stale one. A — Availability: Every request receives a response (not an error), though it might not be the most recent data. The system keeps responding even if some nodes are down. Example: Netflix shows you recommendations even if their recommendation engine is partially down. P — Partition Tolerance: The system continues operating even if network messages are lost or delayed between nodes. A "partition" = network split where nodes can't communicate. In reality: you cannot opt out of P. Networks fail. Partitions happen. You MUST handle partitions. The Real Choice — CP or AP: Since P is mandatory, the real choice is: when a partition occurs, do you sacrifice C or A? CP (Consistency + Partition Tolerance): - When partition happens: refuse to answer rather than return stale data - Some requests get errors during partition - But when you respond, you're always correct - Examples: ZooKeeper, HBase, Google Spanner, MongoDB (with journaling), traditional relational databases AP (Availability + Partition Tolerance): - When partition happens: respond with possibly stale data - System always responds, never returns error - Data might be outdated temporarily - Examples: Cassandra, DynamoDB, CouchDB, DNS Neither CP nor AP fully — just P: - Technically, traditional SQL in a single datacenter: gives up P (can't run across partitions) - Rarely applicable in modern distributed systems Consistency Models (Spectrum): Strong Consistency (Linearizability): - Every read sees the most recent write - As if there's only one copy of data - Slowest — requires synchronization - Example: Google Spanner uses atomic clocks to achieve this globally Sequential Consistency: - All nodes see operations in same order, but might lag - Operations appear instantaneous but may not be truly real-time Causal Consistency: - Causally related operations are seen in order - "If you see my reply, you must have seen my original post" - Used by some distributed databases Eventual Consistency: - If no new updates, all nodes will eventually have the same value - Queries may return stale data temporarily - Highest availability, used by: DynamoDB, Cassandra, S3 - Most common choice for high-scale systems Read-Your-Own-Writes: - You always see your own updates (even if others don't yet) - Instagram: after you post a photo, you see it even

text: LinkedIn & the Origin of Kafka (Case Study) Sources: LinkedIn Engineering Blog, Kreps, Narkhede, Rao — "Kafka: a Distributed Messaging System for Log Processing" (NetDB 2011) The problem LinkedIn had: By the early 2010s, LinkedIn had many separate systems that needed the same underlying activity data — the news feed, search indexing, relevance/ML pipelines, monitoring, and analytics all needed a feed of user activity events (page views, connections made, likes). Each consumer had built its own point-to-point pipeline to get this data, resulting in an N×M mess of custom, fragile integrations between every producer and every consumer. Why existing message queues weren't a fit: Traditional queues (JMS-style brokers) were built for low-throughput, transactional messaging, not the sustained high-throughput firehose of activity events LinkedIn needed to move (hundreds of billions of events/day at LinkedIn's later scale). They also typically delete a message once consumed, so a second, independent consumer couldn't replay the same stream. Kafka's core design choices (as a direct response to that problem): Log-based storage: instead of deleting messages after delivery, Kafka retains them for a configured period (or forever) as an append-only log. Multiple independent consumer groups can each read the same stream at their own pace, tracking their own offset — this single change is what let LinkedIn support many different downstream consumers off one shared pipeline instead of N separate point-to-point integrations. Partitioning: each topic is split into partitions, each handled independently and in order, allowing horizontal scaling of both writes and reads by adding more partitions and consumers. Sequential disk I/O: Kafka relies on sequential reads/writes to disk (fast, even on spinning disks) plus OS page cache, rather than random access — this is why Kafka achieves very high throughput despite persisting everything. Pull-based consumption: consumers pull at their own pace and track their own offset, rather than the broker pushing and needing to track per-consumer state — simplifies the broker and lets slow consumers fall behind without overwhelming themselves, catching up later from their last offset. Outcome: LinkedIn open-sourced Kafka in 2011 and it became an Apache project; it's now the de facto standard for high-throughput event streaming across the industry (adopted by Netflix, Uber, and most large-scale systems that need a durable, replayable, multi-consumer event backbone) — a direct example of solving an internal integration problem generally enough that it became foundational infrastructure well beyond its original use case. Relevance to system design interviews: "Why Kafka over a traditional queue" is a common follow-up question — the answer is precisely this history: replayability (log retention, multiple independent consumer groups) and throughput (partitioning + sequential I/O), not just "it's a queue but faster."

text: Search & Indexing (Inverted Index) Sources: Elasticsearch documentation ("Inverted index"), Apache Lucene documentation What it is: Searching billions of documents for a keyword by scanning each one would be far too slow. Search engines instead build an inverted index ahead of time — a data structure that maps each word to the list of documents containing it — so a search becomes a fast lookup instead of a full scan. Forward index vs inverted index: Forward index: document → list of words it contains (this is the natural way you'd store a document, but useless for "find all docs containing X"). Inverted index: word → list of documents containing it. Flips the mapping so a query for a term is a single lookup, not a scan of every document. Building the index: 1. Tokenization: split text into individual terms ("The quick fox" → ["the", "quick", "fox"]). 2. Normalization: lowercase, remove punctuation, stemming (running → run) so "run", "runs", "running" all match the same index entry. 3. Stop word removal (optional): common words like "the", "is" are often excluded since they match nearly everything and add little search value. 4. For each remaining term, append the document ID (and often position within the document, for phrase search) to that term's posting list. Querying: A search for "quick fox" looks up the posting list for "quick" and for "fox", then intersects them — documents in both lists contain both words. Ranking (which result appears first) typically uses TF-IDF or BM25: term frequency (how often the word appears in this doc) weighted against inverse document frequency (how rare the word is across all docs) — a rare word matching is a stronger signal than a common word matching. Distributed search (how this scales to billions of documents): The full index doesn't fit on one machine. It's split into shards, each holding a subset of documents and its own local inverted index. A query fans out to every shard in parallel, each returns its top-N matches, and a coordinating node merges and re-ranks the combined results — this is exactly how Elasticsearch/Solr scale search across a cluster. Each shard is also typically replicated for both availability and to spread read (query) load across replicas. Real-time-ish updates: New documents don't need a full index rebuild — an update is added as a small new index segment; a background merge process periodically combines small segments into larger ones for query efficiency. This is why "just indexed" documents often show up in search within seconds, not instantly, and why search indexes trade a small delay for much better write throughput. Real-world example: An e-commerce product search: catalog of 50M products is sharded across many nodes. Searching "wireless headphones" fans out to every shard, each returns its best local matches ranked by BM25, coordinator merges and returns the final top 20 — the same pattern used by product search on any major e-commerce site or by Elasticsearch-backed log search internally at a company.

text: LinkedIn & the Origin of Kafka (Case Study) Sources: LinkedIn Engineering Blog, Kreps, Narkhede, Rao — "Kafka: a Distributed Messaging System for Log Processing" (NetDB 2011) The problem LinkedIn had: By the early 2010s, LinkedIn had many separate systems that needed the same underlying activity data — the news feed, search indexing, relevance/ML pipelines, monitoring, and analytics all needed a feed of user activity events (page views, connections made, likes). Each consumer had built its own point-to-point pipeline to get this data, resulting in an N×M mess of custom, fragile integrations between every producer and every consumer. Why existing message queues weren't a fit: Traditional queues (JMS-style brokers) were built for low-throughput, transactional messaging, not the sustained high-throughput firehose of activity events LinkedIn needed to move (hundreds of billions of events/day at LinkedIn's later scale). They also typically delete a message once consumed, so a second, independent consumer couldn't replay the same stream. Kafka's core design choices (as a direct response to that problem): Log-based storage: instead of deleting messages after delivery, Kafka retains them for a configured period (or forever) as an append-only log. Multiple independent consumer groups can each read the same stream at their own pace, tracking their own offset — this single change is what let LinkedIn support many different downstream consumers off one shared pipeline instead of N separate point-to-point integrations. Partitioning: each topic is split into partitions, each handled independently and in order, allowing horizontal scaling of both writes and reads by adding more partitions and consumers. Sequential disk I/O: Kafka relies on sequential reads/writes to disk (fast, even on spinning disks) plus OS page cache, rather than random access — this is why Kafka achieves very high throughput despite persisting everything. Pull-based consumption: consumers pull at their own pace and track their own offset, rather than the broker pushing and needing to track per-consumer state — simplifies the broker and lets slow consumers fall behind without overwhelming themselves, catching up later from their last offset. text: API Gateway Sources: AWS API Gateway Developer Guide, Kong Gateway documentation What it is: A single entry point that sits in front of a collection of backend services (especially in a microservices architecture) and routes each incoming request to the right service. Aggregation: combining calls to multiple services into a single client-facing response (sometimes called the "backend for frontend" pattern) — a mobile app screen might need data from 3 services, gateway can fan out and merge. Observability: single place to log, trace, and monitor all API traffic instead of instrumenting every service separately. TLS termination: gateway handles HTTPS, internal traffic between gateway and services can be plain HTTP within a trusted network. Gateway vs Load Balancer: A load balancer (L4/L7) distributes traffic across replicas of the *same* service based on IP/path. Scale Numbers: - 350+ million monthly active users - 500 million tweets per day (~6000 tweets/second) - 150 million daily active users - Peak: Obama election tweet — 150,000 tweets/second - Average user follows 200 accounts - 1% of users have 1M+ followers (celebrities, news accounts) Core Features to Design: 1. Notifications (likes, retweets, replies) The Hard Problem — Timeline/Feed Generation: Two approaches: Fan-out on Write (push) vs Fan-out on Read (pull) Fan-out on Write (Push Model): - When user A tweets, immediately copy tweet ID to every follower's feed cache - Read is fast — just fetch pre-computed feed from Redis - Problem: if A has 50M followers, writing 50M entries takes too long - Called "hot key" problem — celebrity tweets overwhelm the system Fan-out on Read (Pull Model): - When user opens app, fetch tweets from all accounts they follow - Merge and sort by timestamp - Problem: if following 1000 people, need 1000 queries → too slow Twitter's Hybrid Approach: - Regular users (< 1M followers): Fan-out on write — pre-compute their followers' feeds - Celebrities (1M+ followers): Fan-out on read — their tweets are fetched separately when feed is loaded - Feed = pre-computed feed + lazy-loaded celebrity tweets merged at read time Data Storage: Tweets: - MySQL with Vitess (MySQL clustering) for tweets table - Tweet IDs use Snowflake ID generator (timestamp + machine ID + sequence) — guarantees unique, sortable IDs - Old tweets (>7 days) moved to cold storage (Hadoop/S3) User Relationships (Follow Graph): - Separate social graph service - FlockDB (Twitter's own graph database) or Redis sorted sets - Follow relationship: user_id → set of followed_user_ids - Follower relationship: user_id → set of follower_ids - Both directions maintained for fast lookups Timeline Cache: - Redis — each user has a "home timeline" key with list of tweet IDs (not full tweets) - Stores last 800 tweet IDs per user - Full tweet data fetched from Tweet Store via tweet IDs (separate lookup) - This separation reduces memory usage significantly Media Storage: - Images/videos stored in Blob Storage (S3-equivalent) - Served through CDN globally (Fastly) - Videos transcoded to multiple resolutions on upload (FFmpeg pipeline) - Thumbnails generated asynchronously Tweet Posting Flow: 1.
